item.title: Re: “Green Crabs” they’re always green
item.content:encoded:
Collapsed for ease of scrolling.

+ show block
– hide block

Crabs: Overall I was aiming to connect the crabs with the cancer constellation through the dates of the journal entries being the day that the constellation is represented to the end date that it is represented, I believe I can make this more evident however.

Then how would the constellation’s prevalence relate to the art and the artist’s rage? That seems like another tenuous connection.

Diary Pages: I see what you mean, overall I was aiming to do a slow progression into hatred of the art, but it appears it wasn’t visible, I assume having a distinct part where it appears to be teetering into hatred would make it easier? Overall I presume a reworking would help?

If anything, I’d almost recommend leaning into his self-assurance that this will be his masterpiece. I think you’d be able to make it clear that he dislikes it through over-enthusiastic optimism, if that makes sense.

I have to say, I’m a little confused when it comes to the bit about the paint not sticking to the painting. Is that a motif I’m not getting, or something about the paint that I missed?

Also I aimed to leave the artist’s death to user interpretation either scheele’s green as you mentioned or the first activation of SCP-XXXX-1. The death’s contents can change depending on what the final few diary entries indicate I presume.

I can appreciate the meaningful ambiguity, but at the moment, the ending entry feels a tad anti-climactic. I think that a more carefully handled progression of self-hatred might help with that.

item.content:encoded:
Of the new stuff you've added, I have to say that the end of the new interview might be the most compelling part. At its core, the emotionally compelling elements here are centered around SCPxx's struggle to communicate what it perceives as a terrifying threat. I'd also like to echo my previous recommendation to reconsider some of your redactions. As discussed in MalyceGraves' exceptional guide on the subject, the style you're utilizing here isn't the best way to communicate your plot.

item.title: Re: Brain Coral
item.content:encoded:
this is a pretty solid idea for a memetic kill agent, but I feel like it being THE kill agent for the foundation wouldn't make much sense. It seems like there are multiple memetic kill agents used (scp 1 and scp 2000), so it would be odd for the foundation to let anyone with access to any scp with a kill agent to have access to scp 1. furthermore, this doesn't seem like a thing that can be deleted with amnestics, so if some researcher of an scp with a kill agent needed to edit the article in any way, they would permanently have access to 1, 2000, and every other kill agent. Maybe the kill agent articles are just incredibly incredibly exclusive, but with experimental logs, I'm not too sure about that. The only other problem I have is that it definitely seems like a big scp, and would be difficult to properly write as a second(I'm assuming second from your submissions) scp. Besides that, this is a really nice idea for how memetic kill agents work (besides the exclusivity bit). I would +1 it if you could figure out a way to circumvent the problems I said above.

item.title: Re: My SCP idea
item.content:encoded:
1) If this is negotiating with The Foundation specifically, then that means it has some sapience. This may give The Foundation a reason to try and determine if it can work out a better deal. Even if it's just basically an animal, the reason for targeting The Foundation needs to be explored.

2) Along those lines, an MTF or D-Class may be the wrong idea: The Foundation using this as a prison for its own prisoners or as a way to soften up those it interrogates may be a possibility. This would give the apartment its prisoners and give The Foundation a way to make those it arrests useful beyond any information they may otherwise offer.

Of course, there's nothing to say that the apartment could have an exclusive deal.

3) You need to emphasize the maze-like structure of the apartment. The devil's bargain works (prisoner for info/treasure) but you need to emphasize how hard it is to escape. That would create a much scarier location.

Otherwise, great idea! And your English isn't that bad.

item.title: Re: The Lightswitch
item.content:encoded:
I like this one, especially because of the binary option, but there are some problems:

1) I'm guessing that if you flick it off it takes your personality, if you flick it on you gain all currently absorbed personalities. This is fine, but you may want to put a limit on that if you have multiple personalities in your head only your personality is absorbed and the others are lost. Otherwise, you could potentially have a ridiculous number of personalities.

2) What are the relative strengths of the personalities? Basically, is there a struggle for control, and what kind of power do the other personalities have regarding the actions of the body? Also, are the personalities relegated to the back and can only watch or do they have any kind of voice in what happens?

3) What happens if you flick it on but it doesn't have a personality? What happens if the personality was already given to someone else? Could you absorb another personality and that personality resurrect the body, albeit under new management?

4) While I like the concept, the corpse personality drain may be one step too far. That's the only thing I would suggest dropping.

5) Strictly as a side note, the multiple personalities may actually make the Bookkeeper easier to threaten. Not only is he the receptacle of multiple lives, and thus making him more willing to make a deal; the more personalities the easier he would be to threaten. Also, the personalities may break and at least debate a deal, meaning that the weakest personality would determine if the person breaks.

But otherwise, great concept!

item.title: Cognation
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article

Genre: Horror

Elevator Pitch:

  • A delve into Reality Anchor Construction and Design
  • An Thamiel anomalous SRA Component with strict rules about thinking about; the colour red, wives, or the fear of blood.
  • Additional component used in SRAs being lobotomized reality benders from Project Ichabod
  • Robert Scranton implicated to be the source of this blood.

Central Narrative: The History of the blood being used in SRAs as a Hume lowering component in addition to an advanced state of the blood with hostile telepathic properties. Going onto unravelling the source of the fluid by a researcher and going rogue sending a drone into the origin dimension. Causes a large amount of blood to be converted into the hostile counterpart. Researcher has a tell-all interview with a member of O5 revealing what and who is the source of the blood. Still image of the drone footage is shown and the blood's conversion is happening spontaneously now and will convert all amounts by 20—. O5 Command reclassifying the blood to Keter is pending.

Hook/Attention Grabber: The idea that what if Robert Scranton was the source of this SRA component, the excess humes painfully funneling into the non-dimension, changing the doctor. Turning him into a weak god in the darkness of the abyss, feeding on other gods and becoming hateful of existence itself. Basically what if the Scarlet King is a forgotten echo of a man forced to live and become a god, losing all but his attention on his wife, and waiting to break back into our reality to make existence itself suffer.

Additional Notes: Idea comes from the striking similarities of the beginning of Dust and Blood and the ending of 3001, both barely human entities stuck outside of reality, unable to die, cursed to exist only in red, with their only concern being their wives.

item.title: Brain Coral
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article

Page Layout: Conventional, with containment procedures and description followed by supplemental incident reports and experimental logs. This is followed by a "secret" file with restricted access.

Elevator Pitch: The source of all memetic kill agents used by the foundation, as well as the means of inoculation. A species of coral emits a cognitohazardous vibration that forces cardiac arrest in observers. This vibration remains hazardous in any data form. Polyps separate from the coral and enter an animal's brain, whereupon it becomes immune to the cognitohazard. All high ranking officials of the Foundation are hosting a brain parasite. This coral has formed a symbiotic relationship with the entire foundation. This means YOU have the parasite if you've ever survived the SCP-001 kill agent.

+ show block
– hide block

Central Narrative: The unique effects of the cognitohazard vibration are discovered when security workers are killed viewing the waveform of security footage. Research into its properties and the extent of this effect is undergone. At some point, the idea to use it for security was proposed by the heads of research, Dr. Berryman and Langford, and publicly denied. Shortly after, an "incident" on-site causes the "death" of all coral bushes. In reality, they are quietly moved to an unknown location to implement the memetic security agent.

Hook/Attention-Grabber: My idea is that the true nature of the SCP is hinted at throughout the text before being revealed at the end. The Neutralized classification and description of its supposed destruction should hopefully be somewhat intriguing.

Additional Notes: No idea if this conflicts with any previous articles. As this is my first work and it attempts to retcon something so iconic it may be controversial.

The idea is that the coral will only infect animals that choose not to feed on it, and releases a vibration pulse that travels far underwater and kills all others. This poses the question of what benefit the coral would receive from not simply killing everything around it. Maybe by "whitelisting" certain animals, it can manipulate its ecosystem to evolve beneficially.

Also not sure how the parasite would get in your brain. It would need to enter in a way as to not cause any long-term damage if any at all.

SCP-3000 has proven that the Foundation will utilize anomalies to their benefit, although that is arguably less extreme.


As a courtesy to our readers on mobile devices, please collapse long posts. ~Zyn

item.title: Re: SCP Idea: The Necro-Matriarch Broadcast Manifestations
item.content:encoded:
a mysterious benevolent entity/company is trying to help humanity regain contact with their dead loved ones

I'm admittedly still skeptical about this, since not only does the entity focus on grandmas only for seemingly no reason, the requirement of antique radios doesn't feel conducive to helping humanity as a whole. Would make more narrative sense if, say, you had some anomalous tinkerer who missed his grandma messing with his own radio, which made anomalous broadcasts, which trigger manifestations in other such radios within a certain radius.

+ show block
– hide block

I still like to point out that some articles do have a similar setup as mine, which I took the inspiration from.

Those articles are not your article. Readers voting on your eventual draft are not obligated to look at other successful articles and upvote your work because those articles you did not write are successful. If they don't like your work, they'll downvote, regardless of whether something else has been similar and successful.

Also, I planned this as an initial setup for future articles of mine.

Again, focus on the piece at hand here. If the major plot point of your material is too heavily reliant on future articles, readers might feel like something is missing and the piece comes off more as sloppy rather than mysterious. Remember to keep in mind the readers' point of view—they don't automatically know what's being developed the way you as the author do. If they feel like something is missing, their immediate response is "something is missing" and not "the author must be working on something amazing that hasn't been posted yet".

Yep.

I'm admittedly having trouble believing this, but if you're certain that the audience won't be skeptical, by all means continue.

Oh yeah, that's the right word I am looking for. A tale in a format of what you've said, my bad.

A supplement page is inherently not a tale; it's an offshoot/support page for an SCP article.

item.title: Re: Draft "Disconnected Restroom"
item.content:encoded:
Okay, here goes:

+ show block
– hide block

Immediately from the containment, the information is rather jumbled. Try to structure the containment from establishing the most immediately pertinent visualization aspects first (in this case, the fact that the anomaly is in a provisional site) and then moving from subject to subject for each aspect of requirements (staffing, maintenance, access, etc.). Also, try to trim down the length of the sentences that are simple "don't do this" commands. For example:

It is only to be entered by Level 2 cleared staff and only for research or cleaning purposes.

No water originating from SCP-XXXX is to be used for cleaning and no liquids from outside of SCP-XXX are to be inserted into the facilities.

At no time should SCP-XXXX be used as sanitary facility.

You could just make a quick bullet list with parallel structure so the directions aren't as roundabout. For example:

Personnel accessing SCP-XXXX may not:

  • Enter the anomaly if not performing research or cleaning.
  • Use water produced by SCP-XXXX for cleaning.
  • Insert liquids from outside SCP-XXXX into the facility.
  • Use SCP-XXXX as a sanitary facility.

Remember that clinical tone does not mean using a lot of words to describe something simple. In that same vein, you don't need to use phrases like "at no time" and "at all times" since it's assumed that unless otherwise stated, containment procedures are always in place.

There are also a lot of small errors, such as:

  • Typically authorization levels have hyphens. So Level-2 and not Level 2.
  • Vague instructions. "Cleaning staff are to flush if they hear noises coming from SCP-XXXX" > what exactly are they flushing? What sort of noises?
  • and must make record of doing so. > there should be a standardized log system rather than just "record it somewhere". Ideally, there would be some sort of cleaning report that could be referenced for this sort of thing. "Make record" could be anything from a cell phone call to a post-it note to a formal write-up.
  • I'm not certain if "port-a-potty" would be considered clinical phrasing. "Portable toilet" or "alternative restroom facilities" would be taken more seriously.
  • SCP-XXXX is to be locked at all times unless Level 2 staff requires to enter the SCP. > this should be placed earlier in the instructions. Also, Level-2 staff is a very wide body of individuals; it would make more sense to just note "personnel assigned to SCP-XXXX" or the like. Also, don't refer to an anomaly as "the SCP" (SCP refers to the containment procedures or the Foundation motto). In-universe, the non-slang way to reference this anomaly would just be "SCP-XXXX" or "the restrooms".
  • and so on.

The description is similarly full of small errors in clinical tone and Foundation presentation; the most notable issue is that the anomalous effects are not made immediately clear. There's no need to have the background investigation noted before the effects of drinking the tap water. This is another case where a bullet-point list could be of use, to introduce all of the small anomalous effects together so the reader isn't left wondering why the Foundation bothered containing the location.

The Audio Transcript portion just feels a little sloppily written because the dialogue feels wooden (Frank in particular sounds more like a robot trying to imitate human speech than an actual human talking in the moment) and there are again small errors ("lets" is missing an apostrophe). As a reader, I'm unsure of what the log is meant to convey besides typical "something unknown but bad happened because the place is spooky and something happened to the robot" tension. It feels a little forced and as a result I feel skeptical more than scared.

The Incident Report just feels almost tacked on as an afterthought. I'm not sure why "Michael" needed to be italicized, and the suddenness of the anomaly hurting someone and behaving oddly comes kind of out of nowhere. It would have been better pacing if that sort of effect had been introduced or at least more clearly hinted at in the description. And then at the end of the incident report I as a reader am still unsure about what's going on and why I should care about the anomaly. It messes with people's digestive systems apparently… for what reason? If you don't intend to have an in-universe reason for the manifestation, there needs to at least be a more meaningful takeaway at the end of the article (could have been something like "is the Foundation justified in starving the thing?" or "should the Foundation try to introduce appetite suppressants?") beyond just "okay it can actually do scary things, update the containment".

Overall I feel like the article needs a fair bit of general restructuring so the basic anomaly information and plot flow better. The storyline in particular needs to move more fluidly from the description to the addenda; right now each part feels almost like separate portions of the story with the in-between material removed. As such, it feels jumpy and sudden and disconnected, rather than a followable investigative process of understanding the anomaly.

They bounced off of each other nicely and the dialogue from 5866 had that ancient being flair while not straying far from modern speech patterns.

My main issue with this is the confession log. It feels a bit exposition-dumpy to me. I know that Corbin’s plan had to be explained else 5866 reanimating wouldn’t have made sense, but it felt convenient that she just spills everything out in three paragraphs. Maybe that’s a personal thing and I can’t think of an alternate way you could have potentially done the reveal.

Regardless, I had fun reading this.

item.title: Re: Deus Comedenti (Translation: God Eater)
item.content:encoded:
1. The 'God Eater' thing is part of the narrative. It was originally built with the intention to kill ("Eat") gods. With that in mind, it was designed to contain an entity with great power and convert it into raw unthinking energy. It just so happens that it's current users aren't aware of it's designed purpose and utilize it differently.

2. The machine isn't so much *fed* by death, as it made to transform living human mass. As in once you put a human in and start the process, the mass is broken down to energy, following mass-energy equivalence (E=MC^2). It needs to be human because the runic magic (the machine is an integration of tech and runic magic) was designed to target sentient beings containing akiva, and humans *just* about hit the mark for it to function.

+ show block
– hide block

3. The 'must be stopped' is actually kinda subjective. As in, it helps a country with 1.2 billion people not only avoid spending 12 percent of it's GDP on imports (not to mention that's just the oil %age today, in a world where the oil-energy transition has progressed further, and renewable energy is the big import, it could well be higher), but also provides some income in energy export.
To put things in perspective, that's more than 120 billion dollars freed up to be spent on developing the country, infrastructure, public works (, corruption) etc.

4. I'm actually focusing on two parallel narratives:

-One being the utilization of something admittedly horrific, by a government for something extremely important in a way that the reader can figure out him/herself the importance. In other words, it's 'the greater good' theory, but in a way the reader understands the greater good on an immediate level, while also being aware of the sacrifice.

-The other, more hidden narrative, is the god eater part. I'm not going to outright 'say' the machine was intended to break down gods into pure energy, but I'm going to hint it. Like, the absolute ridiculous amount of energy the machine can store in it's battery, only about a third of which is ever actually utilised by the govt, and a big part of that's maintaining a buffer. How strong the containment circle is warded and etched with ancient runes not commonly seen in use in modern times. I'm also considering having the energy go through a 'Akiva Filter' of sorts, but that might be too obvious. The biggest hint by far, of course, is the name, for those who bother to put it in Google translate.

5. I hope that was enough to answer your bigger concerns. It's an anomaly that breaks down mass to energy (on a surface level), and has a narrative (s) built around that anomoly regarding it's use.


As a courtesy to our readers on mobile devices, please collapse long posts. ~Zyn

Central Narrative: The SCP is a gigantic mass of incorporeal objects located at the center of the earth, the majority of which are human corpses. Various examples will include thaumatology, experimental paratechnology, ghosts and possibly a cameo of that D-Class from SCP-4035. The document ends with a incident report describing a foundation incorporeal object containment unit (like those mentioned in SCP-2996 and SCP-4444) accidently becoming incorporeal and falling into the mass, causing part of it to become corporal before the unit is destroyed, causing part of the earths core to collapse in on itself, creating a minor earthquake. A notice from a foundation scientist reveals that the mass as a whole has been losing incorporeality overtime, with the eventual mass re-solidification of the anomaly leading to disastrous results.

Hook/Attention-Grabber: Taking a semi-used joke to its logical conclusion.

Additional Notes: I am not sure of a reasonable explanation of the masses re-solidification. Is there an established measure of incorporeal energy that the anomaly can be said to be 'shedding'?

item.title: Re: Love at Long Last
item.content:encoded:
(Can't give greenlights)

To start off, I really really like this narrative. Dear Nia is a really great story with themes and technology that would be right at home in the foundation universe. Of course, as has already been noted, the main focus in writing will need to be on changing certain aspects of the story so that it can't be considered plagiarism.

+ Show crit
- Begone crit

…the primary one being that Chase's universe orbits a Red Dwarf while Underwood's earth (our Earth) orbits a Yellow dwarf.

While this does present some really cool imagery, it might need some minor explanation in the article, as the earth would be a very different place if it were orbiting a red dwarf. Orbiting a different class of star but still resulting in nearly identical timelines is a bit of a stretch beyond the multiverse theory. If you wanted to keep Chase's sun a Red Dwarf, perhaps you could explain by saying the mass of the sun was changed due to advance foundation testing or anomalies in that dimension? Ultimately though, this is only likely to be noticed by astro and quantum physics nerds like me and won't detract from the narrative.

This leads to an event known as "Gothic Storm", the first known Reality-Merging Class Scenario (RMK-Class) in that reality. The aftermath is chaotic, and leads to public awareness of the Foundation, the release of numerous anomalies, and shifts of entire galaxies in the universe.

I really like these consequences, as it does something the original story doesn't: showing the direct consequences of not letting go. However, since reality ending scenarios don't carry much weight in a narrative like this, perhaps also having a more personal consequence could give the narrative more of a punch. Perhaps either Underwood or Chase has a child, but due to Underwood's persistence in contacting Chase, the collapsing realities causes the death of the child. This gives us a more emotional and relatable consequence to Underwood not being able to let go and could show her that her actions have only caused more suffering to those she has left. This would also help set this story apart from Dear Nia.

Dr. Underwood had seemingly disappeared, while Dr. Chase was discovered in her office. The document ends with an interview with Chase, and remains the only documentation of this event.

While this does give the narrative some mystery and a feeling of being unresolved, it feels a bit out of place. IMO, Underwood should not disappear, or at least be allowed to at least give a final log or message that shows us whether she's realized the weight and consequences of her actions or not. This could help wrap up the story's theme and transition better into the interview with Chase.

With a few minor tweaks, I would definitely give this a greenlight if I could.

Hey ResearcherRando, thanks for bringing these issues up. If we could get some clarification on one of your points, that'd be great.

+ Snipped for mobile users
– hide block

I think the ability for more freedom in trying to convey what makes an idea worth it could benefit this site greatly. Once again: this spot isn’t impossible, but cam present real problems to someone in trying to cram an idea into a small format.

What are you suggesting we change, specifically? That we raise the word count limit on idea posts? Authors have a number of resources at their disposal already to receive crit which aren't encumbered by a word limit, whether that's the IRC chatrooms, a couple trusted Discord servers, or other avenues.1 Moreover the greenlighting process isn't mandatory for posting to the site — it's only a requirement in order to use the draft forum.

With that said, authors seems pretty free to mix and match what styles of critique work for them.

For a site requiring hard work from new creators, all it takes is ten people deciding to press a button saying they didn’t like it, and that says to the author this page is worthy of deletion.

Bit of a correction here: the -10 deletion threshold means that ten more people downvote the page than upvote it, not that ten people overall downvote.

in trying to add to something I’ve seen as fun and a little silly, I’ve been met with an incredibly high wall, in some ways earned by the site, but in many ways just as ridiculous.

I agree, it takes a lot of work to get something to stick on this site. If you're driven to see your idea(s) succeed, we encourage you to continue working on them up-until-and-beyond the point that they'll stay on the site. This site's high standards are meant as less of an impassible boundary and more as a motivator.

Footnotes
1. The word limit was initially put in place at the request of critters — before it was implemented, ideas tended to be exceedingly long and directionless. The rule intends to force new authors to streamline their ideas and make them look more appealing to critters (moreso than giant walls of text, anyways). Personally I think 400 words is rather generous.
